extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (counsel preparing jury instructions); secondary: jurors as recipients of instructions
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent litigation: judge-facing guidance and ready-to-use jury language covering claim construction, infringement (literal and equivalents), invalidity (prior art, anticipation, obviousness), damages, willfulness, and related procedural points. Designed to be customized to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality and tailoring of Instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the fundamental goals of the Instructions is to provide a neutral set of jury instructions that would not be biased in favor of either the patent owner or the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions are not intended to address every conceivable issue; litigants must tailor the Instructions to particular facts and legal issues and eliminate superfluous or confusing instructions. Use these Instructions in conjunction with other, non-patent-specific instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bracketed terminology for customization
rubrics_metrics.description: To enhance litigants' ability to customize the Instructions to a particular case, bracketed terminology (e.g., [subject matter], [the Defendant], [claims in dispute]) is provided so parties can find-and-replace case-specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brackets indicate where alternative terminology may be used (e.g., [[product] [method]]). Users should replace placeholders (e.g., 'system' -> 'product') and make appropriate edits for product vs method patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Notes (guidance not to be read to jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Notes are provided throughout the Instructions to assist judges and counsel; they are not statements of law and are not to be included in the jury instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Notes provide practical insights based on judges' and counsel's experience (e.g., when to give a means-plus-function instruction, how to avoid jury confusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary instruction: Nature of the action and the parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain to jurors that this is a patent case, identify patents at issue, briefly describe the technology, and advise that a glossary of technical terms will be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell jurors the plaintiff is the patent owner and defendant is the accused; familiarize jurors with patent basics so they can follow evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States Patents—what a patent is and how it is obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the United States or importing it. A patent application includes a specification and claims; the Patent Examiner searches prior art and issues Office Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain prosecution history (file wrapper), role of PTO/Patent Examiner, what claims do (define scope), and that jury will be instructed on what constitutes prior art in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent litigation overview—infringement and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may sue to stop alleged infringing acts or recover damages. The patent owner must prove infringement and the amount of damages; an accused infringer may assert invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that a patent is presumed valid but that presumption can be overcome with clear and convincing evidence; differentiate burdens of proof for infringement vs invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof standards (preponderance vs clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner must prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence; the party challenging validity must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jury-friendly explanations of standards: preponderance ~ more likely than not (>50%); clear and convincing = highly probable; note difference from 'beyond a reasonable doubt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentions of the parties—plaintiff's burden to prove infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] contends that [the Defendant] imports, makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells a [[product] [method]] that infringes [claim(s) in dispute]; [The Plaintiff] must prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doctrine of equivalents not in issue, modify to omit. The jury must compare accused product/method to each asserted claim individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two pathways to direct infringement: literal and doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways a patent claim can be directly infringed: (1) literal infringement and (2) infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge will instruct claim meanings; jury must use judge's constructions. Distinguish literal vs equivalents and instruct jury which path is at issue in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement—each and every claim element required
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every [[element] [method step]] in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused product lacks one or more claim elements, there is no literal infringement; decide literal infringement claim-by-claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents—insubstantial differences (function-way-result)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product/method contains the equivalent of each claim element not literally present—i.e., an element that is only insubstantially different, often shown by performing substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that equivalents exist for each missing element; jury should be instructed on recognized limitations to the doctrine (see prosecution history estoppel, dedication to public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents—prosecution history estoppel and dedication to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations on the doctrine include prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public, which can bar application of equivalents for certain claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instructions on how prosecution amendments or statements may limit equivalents; give examples and relevant case citations as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction—general (judge defines claim terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's job to give the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted; jurors must accept and use those meanings when deciding infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are to be construed the same way for infringement and invalidity; read stipulations and the court's claim constructions to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction for the case—read court constructions/stipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]; the judge provides constructions of disputed terms and of any limitations governed by 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6 (means-plus-function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Teva v. Sandoz, Phillips, Markman, etc., and explain that jurors must follow the court’s constructions even if they disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims—construction and limiting structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim element is expressed as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function (35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6), the element covers the structure or steps described in the specification that perform the recited function and equivalents, not all means that perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction 2.2 should be given only if the case involves means-plus-function claims; judge should identify the recited function and the corresponding structure/step in the specification (or equivalents) for jury use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement analysis—compare accused product/method to claims (not plaintiff product)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement, the jury must compare the accused product/method to the claims of the patent; you may not compare the accused product to the plaintiff's commercial product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims infringed directly vs indirectly and literally vs under doctrine of equivalents; for indirect infringement, distinguish induced vs contributory infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—knowledge and intent are immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement does not require knowledge of the patent or intent to infringe; such mental state is immaterial to the finding of direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction clarifies that direct infringement is a question of whether the accused product/method meets the claim limitations, regardless of defendant's awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement—actively inducing and contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement includes inducing another to infringe (active inducement) and contributory infringement (supplying a component especially made for use in a patented invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate instructions on elements required for inducement and contributory infringement, including required knowledge and intent where applicable (e.g., intent to induce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §271(f)(1) and §271(f)(2) (supply of components abroad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement can occur by supplying all or a substantial portion of components of a patented invention for assembly abroad (§271(f)(1)), or by supplying components especially made/adapted for use in the patented invention abroad (§271(f)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge should instruct jury on the specific statutory elements and any factual disputes regarding supply, substantiality, and special adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §271(g) (product made by a patented process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may be liable for infringement by import, sale, offer for sale, or use of a product made by a patented process (§271(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the nexus between the product and the asserted process claim and the elements required for §271(g) liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions discuss infringement as it applies to dependent claims and how to assess infringement when dependent claims add limitations to independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind jurors to evaluate each claim individually and apply claim constructions consistently across independent and dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim phrase meanings: 'comprising of', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: Special instructions are provided regarding how to treat transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'consisting of', and 'consisting essentially of' in claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain to jurors how each transitional term affects claim scope (open vs closed vs partially open) with examples as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense—overview
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury must decide whether the defendant has proven that asserted claims are invalid, overcoming the presumption of validity with clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity can be based on prior art (anticipation, obviousness), written description/enablement failures, or other statutory bars; instruct on the specific invalidity theories asserted in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art—definitions (pre-AIA vs AIA) and what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is defined differently under pre-AIA and AIA law: pre-AIA categories (e.g., date of invention, one-year bars) vs AIA (publicly available before effective filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note on 'Cutoff Date' explains that Cutoff Date may vary by claim and by pre-AIA vs AIA subsections; jury may need instruction on determining Cutoff Date(s) for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art considered or not considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury should be instructed whether certain prior art was considered by the Patent Examiner and what that may mean for invalidity contentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain differences between art considered by examiner and newly presented art, and appropriate weight (but avoid suggesting examiner's conclusions are dispositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions discuss how invalidity findings relate to independent and dependent claims and how to apply invalidity theories to each claim individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind jurors to assess each challenged claim on the applicable invalidity theory, using the same claim constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'person of ordinary skill in the art' (pre-AIA vs AIA timing) as the level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by persons working in the area at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POSITA definition is central to obviousness and enablement inquiries; provide factual indicia for jurors to consider when evaluating level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—prior public knowledge, public use, on-sale bar, printed publication, prior invention, prior patent, prior U.S. application
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation instructions cover many ways a claim can be anticipated: prior public knowledge, prior public use, on-sale bar (including pre-AIA/AIA distinctions), experimental use, printed publications, prior patents, and prior U.S. applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate sub-instructions for pre-AIA vs AIA contexts where relevant; instruct jurors on elements required to prove anticipation for each category and how to treat experimental uses and printed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Graham factors and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness instructions follow Graham v. John Deere: (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between claimed invention and prior art, (3) level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations) such as commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how jurors should weigh these factors together and the standard for proving obviousness (clear and convincing evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. §112)—sufficiency of specification to teach making and using
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement requires the specification to describe how the invention works and how to make and use it so as to enable others skilled in the art to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors on what evidence is relevant to enablement (breadth of claim vs enabling disclosure) and burden of proof for invalidity based on non-enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention sufficient to show that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain differences between written description and enablement, and instruct jurors on how to evaluate written description challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—general (statutory basis and issues to decide)
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine damages the patent owner has proven. Damages are governed by 35 U.S.C. § 284 and include lost profits and reasonable royalty among other considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline phases: date damages begin, types of damages, apportionment, and burdens of proof for damages elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin—stipulated vs disputed start date
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions provide alternatives for when the damages period begins: Alternate A (stipulated date) and Alternate B (when start date is disputed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disputed, instruct jury how to determine appropriate start date based on evidence and relevance to damages calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of damages—lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: List and define recoverable damages types: lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, and reasonable royalty (among others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide elements and evidentiary requirements for each damages type (e.g., Panduit factors for lost profits) and how to quantify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—smallest salable unit and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties should be based on the 'smallest salable unit' that practices the patent and has close relation to the claimed invention; where that unit contains non-infringing features, damages must be apportioned to the value attributable to the patented technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entire market value rule (EMV) is a narrow exception: patentee must show the patented feature 'drives the demand' or 'substantially creates the value' of the entire product to recover royalties on entire product revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—multiple patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement of multiple patents is found, separate royalties may be awarded for each patent; jurors may consider number of licenses needed and effect on hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of stacking licenses and how multiple patents affect the reasonable royalty negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—timing (hypothetical negotiation and hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are based on what parties would have agreed at the hypothetical negotiation date, not on hindsight; but jurors may consider information the parties would have foreseen or estimated, which sometimes includes post-infringement evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List cases and examples of admissible post-hypothetical evidence (e.g., subsequent licenses, profits, non-infringing alternatives) and caution against improper hindsight distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—availability and cost of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider evidence about acceptable non-infringing substitutes and their cost when determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define what constitutes an acceptable substitute (licensed under the patent or non-infringing) and weight the evidence accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—use of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider amounts paid in other license agreements for the same or similar technologies, but must account for differences between those licenses and the hypothetical license at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license need not be perfectly comparable to be considered; adjust for differences in technologies, economic circumstances, and contracting parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMV) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: EMV is a narrow exception to the apportionment rule: to base royalties on entire product revenues, patentee must establish the patented feature drives demand or substantially creates the product's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Federal Circuit authority and instruct jurors to apply EMV only when its strict requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts about damages resolved against infringer due to poor recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts jurors may have on damages due to the defendant's failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusion or difficulty caused by defendant's records should be held against defendant; cite Sensonics, Lam cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND-specific guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, jury should be instructed on the particulars of the patentee's FRAND commitment, on patent law principles, and only on relevant Georgia-Pacific factors; jurors must be instructed on apportionment to the portion of the standard and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not instruct on irrelevant Georgia-Pacific factors; explain apportionment between value of standard and value of claimed invention (Ericsson, Apple v. Motorola guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, jurors must determine whether infringement was willful; plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether defendant's conduct was malicious, wanton, deliberate, consciously wrongful, flagrant, or in bad faith, but knowledge alone is insufficient. Assess totality of circumstances and defendant's knowledge at the time of challenged conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—reliance on legal opinion and §298 limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA (35 U.S.C. § 298) eliminated failure to obtain an opinion of counsel as a factor for willfulness; while a reasonable reliance on a competent legal opinion may be considered if claimed by defendant, the absence of such opinion does not permit an inference of willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify instruction based on whether defendant asserts reliance on counsel. Explain applicability of §298 and the technical correction extending §298 to cases filed after January 14, 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury procedure and trial phases (six phases explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the six phases of a jury trial: (1) jury selection (completed), (2) opening statements, (3) presentation of evidence, (4) closing arguments, (5) final jury instructions, and (6) jury deliberations and verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the nature of opening/closing statements (not evidence), deposition testimony equivalence, and the need to keep an open mind until all evidence is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use same claim meaning for infringement and invalidity; consider each claim individually
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors must use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity analyses, and must consider each claim individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize consistency in applying court’s claim constructions across issues and claims.
